item.title: Takachiho Gorge — Guide
item.description: Takachiho Gorge, in the mountains of northern Miyazaki, is one of Japan’s most stunning natural landscapes. Formed when ancient lava from Mount Aso cooled and was carved by the Gokase River, the narrow gorge is walled by dramatic columns of grey volcanic basalt, rising up to 100 metres in beautifully symmetrical, folded formations. Down the middle flows the emerald-green river, and the slender Manai Falls tumbles some 17 metres directly into the gorge — the iconic view.

item.title: Takachiho Shrine — Guide
item.description: Takachiho Shrine (Takachiho Jinja), founded some 1,900 years ago, is the spiritual heart of the mythologically rich town of Takachiho in northern Miyazaki. Set in a serene, atmospheric grove of towering ancient cedar trees, the weathered wooden shrine radiates a deep sense of age and sanctity. Among its treasures is a magnificent pair of 800-year-old ‘meoto sugi’ (husband-and-wife cedar trees), joined at the roots, around which couples walk hand in hand for blessings of love, marriage and harmony.

item.title: Takachiho's Sacred Caves — Guide
item.description: The Takachiho area is home to sacred caves at the very heart of Japan’s foundational creation mythology, making them among the most spiritually charged natural sites in the country. The most famous is linked to the legend of Amaterasu, the sun goddess, who — angered by her brother — hid herself in a heavenly rock cave (Ama-no-Iwato), plunging the world into darkness until the other gods gathered to lure her out.

item.title: Tateba Shrine — Guide
item.description: Miyazaki (historically Hyuga) is deeply woven into Japan’s founding mythology as the land from which the legendary first emperor, Emperor Jimmu, is said to have set out on his eastern expedition to found the nation. Small shrines along the coast, such as Tateba Shrine, are tied to these ancient legends, marking places connected to Jimmu and the gods of the creation myths. Atmospheric and steeped in history, such a shrine offers a quiet, contemplative stop away from the busier sights: weathered wooden buildings, a torii gate, a coastal or wooded setting, and a palpable sense of the deep mythological roots that run through this part of Kyushu.

item.title: Udo Shrine — Guide
item.description: Udo Shrine (Udo Jingū), on the rugged Nichinan coast south of Miyazaki, is one of Kyushu’s most unusual and scenic shrines, set inside a large cave in the seaside cliffs. Reached by a walking path down through vermilion torii gates along the crashing coastline, the shrine’s brightly coloured main hall stands within the mouth of the ocean cave, the waves surging against the rocks just below — a spectacular, atmospheric setting.
